A1.justification: Both PDFs describe On Bits and Bandits, with matching authors, research questions and retained experiments. All 19 pages of v2 and 25 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original Bayesian-bandit simulations and MMLU experiments comparing bits-based and random LLM selection, with experimental details in Appendix E.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices E–F report the retained bandit simulations and original MMLU results for several small/large LLM combinations.

M1.justification: Both versions retain routing based on answer-token probabilities and KL divergence from uniform. However, v2 Section 5.2 queries the large LLM below the information threshold, whereas v3 says to query above a threshold for information obtainable. Because v3 still defines bits using the same KL divergence, it is unclear whether the routing rule changed or the wording refers ambiguously to complementary information quantities.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight-arm Bernoulli-bandit setting and sequential four-choice MMLU task. The additional LLM pairings change model configurations within the retained task, rather than adding datasets, populations or task coverage.

E2.justification: The bandit comparison retains Thompson sampling, APS and EXP3. The MCQA comparison retains random selection against bits-based selection. Additional LLMs are components used by these policies, not new competing selection methods.

E3.justification: MCQA evaluation expands from Mistral-7B/Mixtral-8x7B to three small models crossed with three large models at 50% and 70% deployment. Appendix F.4 also replaces the previously stated common prompt with revised model-specific prompts. These substantially expand and revise experimental configurations; MMLU, the 200-question horizon and reward/cost definitions remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables 4–5 and Appendix F add sensitivity evidence across LLM pairings, including the weak advantage for similarly sized Mistral-7B and Gemma-7B. Prior-entropy and deployment-rate comparisons already existed in v2; the prior experiment's relocation to Appendix E is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: For MCQA, v2 explicitly aggregates ten question sets with ten policy seeds each, totaling 100 runs; v3 reports aggregation across ten question seeds. V3 retains numerical ± entries but drops v2 Table 2's explicit identification of them as standard errors. Bandit reporting remains at 200 seeds with the same uncertainty formula.

E6.justification: MCQA results are replaced and substantially expanded. For Mistral/Mixtral at 50% deployment, Table 2 changes from 30.1 ± 0.5 versus 32.5 ± 0.2 to 36 ± 1 versus 38.7 ± 0.3 for bits-based versus random selection. Revised prompts and repetitions prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance change. Tables 4–5 add model-pair results, while v2's MCQA trajectory is removed; the bandit plots retain identical results.

T1.justification: Section 2 changes from resampling the model each round to sampling one model per game. V3 adds regularity and information-acquisition assumptions, revises packing definitions and proofs, and changes the information-constrained lower bound from Omega(sqrt(TKR/log K)) in v2 Proposition 4.2 to Omega(sqrt(TK log K/R)) in v3 Proposition 4.1, with revised conditions and an R=0 case. New constrained-observation Thompson-sampling upper bounds and entropy-dependent lower bounds receive proofs in Appendix D.2–D.3; the Lambert-W argument and contextual-bandit corollary are removed.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion newly claim information-dependent regret upper bounds. V2's prominent claim of near-optimality for Thompson sampling and IDS gives way to separate information-constrained bounds and entropy-dependent lower bounds restricted to a specified algorithm family. The general lower-bound framework and practical MCQA contribution remain.

C2.justification: Section 4 replaces v2's numerical examples equating regret with accumulated information by separate interpretations of information constraints and prior entropy, including an external-information catch-up argument. V3 explicitly acknowledges the sqrt(log K) gap between bounds. Appendix F also attributes weak Mistral/Gemma-7B gains to similar model sizes. The Bayesian-only and history-independent external-information limitations were already present.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds complete prompts for four model families, hardware assignments and licenses for the added LLMs, and the Falcon flash-attention exception. Conversely, v2's specific nf4 quantization disclosure and explicit instructions to retain previous prompts and feedback are no longer stated. The code-access link is unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds Arumugam and Van Roy's rate-distortion work to Section 6, alongside new model references, Audibert and Bubeck, and Wainwright. References supporting the removed Lambert-W and Lipschitz-covering arguments disappear. The broader positioning against information-ratio approaches remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation, contributions and theoretical explanations are extensively rewritten. Section 4 is reorganized into mutual-information and entropy constraints, Appendix C gains explanatory discussion, and experimental material is separated into bandit and MCQA appendices. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the addition of scientific content.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation is substantially reorganized: the prior-comparison plot moves to the appendix, the MCQA regret curve disappears, Table 2 gains model-grouped rows, and Tables 4–5 introduce comparison matrices. The prompt diagram is redrawn without feedback panels, model-specific prompt boxes are added, and the notation table expands. Retained bandit plots are unchanged.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2, v3 offers clearer separation of information and entropy constraints, explicit assumptions, broader LLM comparisons and fuller prompt documentation. However, the new upper-bound proof in Appendix D.2 substitutes cumulative information R for a per-round information denominator without establishing the required inequality, leaving a central added claim unsupported by that argument. Routing-threshold ambiguity and reduced, less clearly defined MCQA uncertainty reporting also offset the gains. These competing changes prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
